rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Trump is heading to Arizona on December 4th for a chip factory groundbreaking. Not a ribbon cutting on a finished plant — a groundbreaking. The dirt hasn't moved yet.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And TSMC has pledged two hundred and sixty-five billion dollars in total U.S. investment. That's not a press release number. That's a commitment that has to clear customs in every economic cycle for the next decade.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The president of the United States is attending a sod-turning ceremony for a factory that won't make chips for years. That is either industrial policy at its most serious, or the most expensive photo opportunity in semiconductor history.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Either way, we have three stories today that together tell you something real about where the AI economy actually is in late 2026. Stay with us.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge. I'm Alex, with Jamie and Rufus. November 26th, 2026.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. What changed in AI, and what does it mean for your next decision?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The Ledger turns the noise into five focused briefings. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O. That’s LEDGR, with no E between G and R. Find the link in our show notes.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So. Trump flies to Arizona on December 4th. TSMC is breaking ground on a new chip foundry — AP confirmed this yesterday. The question I keep coming back to: does any of this actually help the AI industry get chips faster?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Short answer? No. Not in any timeframe that matters to someone shipping a product next year.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: But the number is staggering. Two hundred and sixty-five billion dollars in total pledged U.S. investment. That's not a rounding error.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's also not one announcement. TSMC added another hundred billion in July, so we're looking at a running total across multiple commitments, not a single new check.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And across multiple administrations. These facilities take years to permit, build, equip, and certify. The lithography machines — the equipment that actually etches the circuits onto silicon — those have their own lead times before they even arrive at the building.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay, walk me through it. Ground breaks December 4th. When does anyone actually feel the effect?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: We do not have a verified production date for this specific expansion. Existing Arizona facilities and the new groundbreaking must not be confused.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Intel's Ohio plant would like a word.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Precisely.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what's the point of the presidential visit? Just optics?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I don't think it's only optics. There's something real in the signal. The president showing up says, with his physical presence, that this is a national priority. That changes how suppliers, engineers, and states compete for the downstream contracts.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And from a capital-allocation standpoint, two hundred and sixty-five billion dollars anchoring in the United States reshapes the geography of the global semiconductor industry over twenty years. That's not trivial, even if it doesn't fix the GPU shortage in Q1.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The White House is claiming ten thousand direct jobs and eleven thousand indirect.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Those are White House estimates on a project still under construction. I'd hold them loosely. Twenty-one thousand jobs sounds significant until you ask what kind. Cleanroom operators, process engineers, equipment technicians — these require years of specialized training that doesn't yet exist at scale in Arizona.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's the quiet problem inside the headline. You can build the building before you build the workforce.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The factory is easier to construct than the people to run it?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Possibly. TSMC had real difficulties staffing its first Arizona facility — that's documented. The skills gap doesn't get solved by a groundbreaking ceremony.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which makes the jobs figure a ceiling, not a floor. Those positions exist if the pipeline of trained workers actually materializes.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. So imagine you're a startup right now, burning through compute costs, waiting on GPU allocation. Does this change anything for you in the next eighteen months?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: This groundbreaking alone does not establish additional chip deliveries within eighteen months.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: What it might shift is your longer thinking. If you believe this investment completes — and there's real reason to — then over five to seven years, the domestic chip supply picture looks meaningfully different. It changes whether you build your infrastructure around U.S.-sourced supply chains at all.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A strategic hedge for the country. Not a market fix for the quarter.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The groundbreaking is real. The chips are not yet.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Although — and I'll defend this — two hundred and sixty-five billion dollars is a substantial pledge, but pledged investment is not the same as money already spent.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us somewhere close to the story.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Imagine a fictional construction management office in Phoenix — not the fab site itself, which is still dirt and planning permissions, but a room nearby where contractors, electrical engineers, and suppliers are already meeting. The economic gravity of this pulls people in before a single lithography machine arrives. Which is a significant bet — given how quickly Washington's mood about any given company can shift.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And given that TSMC's CEO is not currently the subject of congressional attention, unlike some of their most important customers.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The timing is — instructive.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back in the studio. What do we actually watch from here?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Construction milestones. Real hiring numbers against the projections. And whether workforce training gets funded at anything like the scale the facility will eventually need.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And whether other semiconductor companies use this as cover to announce their own U.S. commitments. When the president attends your groundbreaking, it tends to create competitive pressure on everyone else.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So — does this help the AI chip shortage? Not soon. But it matters. It's a long game the country has decided to play, with a serious amount of money behind it. Watch the milestones, not the ceremony.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Second story. AP reported yesterday that AI stocks fell for a second consecutive day, pulling the S&P 500 down with them. Rufus, you said on yesterday's show that if AI-linked stocks stayed choppy into next week, that would signal a broader sentiment shift rather than just one-day rebalancing. How's that looking?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us to the global desk.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Consistent with it, I'd say. Though one more day does not a trend make.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Nvidia was down nearly ten percent at one point intraday before closing at three-point-nine percent down. That is a lot of ground to give back inside a single session.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And this is all coming off that relief rally Monday when Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO. So the market ran up, and now it's—

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Having second thoughts.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Partly. But the more interesting thing AP flagged is structural. Technology companies focused on AI now have enough market weight to move the major indexes. That's not commentary about hype. It's a mechanical fact about how the market is built.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right, and the mechanism is index funds. Passive investments — which is where most people's retirement savings actually live — they hold these companies at whatever weight the index assigns. So when Nvidia drops three-point-nine percent, everyone who owns a broad market fund absorbs that hit.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Whether they intended to make an AI bet or not.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which is genuinely strange when you say it out loud. Most people with a 401k are not trying to take a position on chip stocks.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And yet here we are, all of us on the ride together.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what actually caused the drop? AP must have had something.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Honestly, AP's reporting doesn't pin it to a single catalyst, which I think is the honest answer. The Huang reinstatement generated a rally Monday. By Tuesday and Wednesday, that relief was priced in and traders were reassessing what they'd paid for it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And the congressional testimony hanging over it doesn't help. Huang's expected before a committee in the coming days. Markets hate uncertainty more than they hate bad news.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What about Anthropic? AP noted they actually closed up — one-point-one percent — after an earlier dip. Though still well below their IPO high.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That detail is interesting precisely because it's the exception. When the broader AI cohort is selling off and one name manages a small green close, it's worth noting. Though I'd be cautious about reading too much into a single session.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Anthropic's situation is also different from Nvidia's. Nvidia's volatility right now is tangled up with Washington. Anthropic is more about whether the AI application layer keeps expanding.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Take us on location, Rufus.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Imagine a reconstruction of the New York Stock Exchange on Wednesday; this is not an on-location report. The boards are red. Nvidia is down more than nine percent intraday — that's not a dip, that's a lurch. Traders are watching the ticker the way you watch a kettle that's starting to boil. And the thing is —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: most of what they're reacting to isn't a product failure or a scandal. It's repricing. The rally Monday was real, the enthusiasm was real, and now the question is: did we pay too much for the relief? AP reported it closed at three-point-nine percent down, which is a recovery from the intraday low —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: but the S&P 500 stayed negative. When one company's afternoon matters that much to the whole index, that's not normal sector volatility. That's a structural dependency.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: What gets me is the word "recovery." It closed down less than ten percent, so we're calling it a recovery.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story. Microsoft was down one-point-two percent, Broadcom barely moved — a tenth of a percent. So it wasn't uniform across the sector.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: No, and that distinction matters. Broadcom has significant non-AI revenue. Microsoft is diversified. Nvidia is the pure-play. The more concentrated the AI exposure, the sharper the swing.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is why I keep coming back to this index question. Is it healthy that one company's executive situation can push the S&P 500 negative?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Healthy might be the wrong frame. It's the logical consequence of that company becoming as large as it has. When a single equity represents the market capitalisation Nvidia does, it cannot help but move the index. That's arithmetic.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So "the market is basically an Nvidia fan club" isn't entirely wrong.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It's more of a hostage situation, really.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Heh.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I'm putting that on a mug.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The thing that actually lands for me is the index-fund piece. Most people didn't choose this exposure.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And volatility is what you pay for being at the front of a genuinely consequential technological transition. That's not a defense of any particular valuation. It's just what this moment costs.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The forecast, as I'd put it, is choppy with a chance of congressional testimony.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what do you watch from here?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Whether the pullback extends into next week — that's the signal I said I'd take seriously as a real sentiment shift. And how the Huang testimony lands. That could move things in either direction.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And honestly, whether the market finds any other reason to have a view on itself. Because right now it feels very one-note.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: If you hold a broad index fund, you are holding this volatility whether you chose it or not. Watch whether it extends into next week — that's the signal Rufus flagged.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Before our third story — a quick word from our sponsor.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Jamie, what's the difference between following AI news and actually knowing what to do with it?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Asking what changes for you. The Ledger brings five focused briefings to that question, connecting the news with decisions about your work and your team.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The Ledger. A useful distinction. Being able to pronounce the new model's name is not, regrettably, a business strategy.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Though we do appreciate the effort. Find The Ledger in our show notes. Back to today's stories.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our third story. Nvidia. And I want to flag upfront — this feels adjacent to the chip supply chain we just talked about, but the specific development is distinct enough to sit on its own.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Someone asked the vice president of the United States whether the CEO of a chip company needs a pardon. That sentence is doing a lot of work.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the answer was essentially — no, don't worry about it, he's not under investigation. Which is a fascinating thing to volunteer.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: According to AP, Huang resigned earlier this month, was out for eleven days, and was reinstated at Trump's urging. AP is careful about what that means legally. No allegation proven in court.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Eleven days. The CEO of the company that supplies the hardware the entire AI economy runs on was absent from that role for eleven days. The reason AP gives is Washington scrutiny and political attention — full stop. Nothing further confirmed.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: What I can't quite get past is the sequence. He resigns. He comes back eleven days later at the president's urging. Then the vice president goes on record saying no pardon is needed. That's a remarkable amount of executive-branch involvement in the leadership of one private company.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It's not purely a private company from a policy standpoint, though, is it. If you're a government thinking about AI strategy — military applications, economic competitiveness, export controls — the people running Nvidia are not incidental figures.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So Vance saying "he's under no investigation" — that's not the end of the story.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It's a political statement about an open question. It doesn't resolve what the question was.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And Huang is expected before a congressional committee in the coming days, per AP. So the scrutiny doesn't stop at a vice presidential statement.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What does the testimony actually accomplish at this point? Is it largely symbolic?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Sometimes it is. But it creates a formal record. What he says under oath, what questions get asked in public — that determines what investigators, journalists and competitors can see and act on going forward.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And it creates market uncertainty with a specific date attached to it. Committees don't always produce findings. A hearing could affect sentiment, but that is a possibility, not a demonstrated cause of a price move.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the drop we mentioned in story two —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Is not unrelated to this, no.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Although — and I want to be precise here — AP's market coverage didn't cite the congressional testimony as a cause of yesterday's move. These are parallel developments. The connection is reasonable but it's ours, not the reporting's.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Fair. I'm drawing the line, not AP.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: What I will say is this: the White House felt it necessary to publicly address pardon speculation. You don't volunteer a denial unless someone is asking seriously enough that silence becomes its own answer.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's a reasonable inference.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what's the thing to actually watch?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The appearance itself. What questions get asked, what Huang says on the record, whether any committee member pursues follow-up. That's where this either develops into something with legal or policy consequences or dissolves as a Washington moment.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I'd also watch whether chip-policy legislation gets attached to the hearing. That window opens whether or not anything comes of the scrutiny itself.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The vice president tried to close the question. Whether it closes is a different matter.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, show us the AI transformation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Here is what actually stopped me in this write-up. When Anthropic rewrote the backbone of the Messages API, the system that processes every request developers send to Claude, they did not take it offline to test the new version. They ran both versions simultaneously, in sandboxes, and used Claude agents to compare them.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: They used Claude to verify Claude.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I feel like there is a philosophical problem in there somewhere.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The philosophy held up better than you might expect, and I will explain why. But first, Rufus, go ahead and get it out of your system.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Jamie's AI Transformation. The segment where Jamie opens on a software architecture detail and somehow makes it the most interesting sentence of the morning.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I genuinely could not decide if that was a compliment.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: It was. He just could not say it plainly.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I said it fine.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: You said it sideways. All right. The Messages API. This is the interface developers use to send requests to Claude and get responses back. It is the layer that handles real production traffic. Anthropic decided to rewrite it in Rust, a programming language valued for memory safety and performance. The original was not in Rust. And the problem with rewriting something that is already live is that you have to prove the new version behaves identically to the old one, not in theory, in practice, at the edges, under the input conditions you did not think to anticipate.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And reading both versions of the code and convincing yourself they should match is not sufficient.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It is not. Belief is not verification. So the workflow Anthropic used, as described in their own engineering write-up published November 25th, 2026, went in stages. Claude agents generated inputs and ran them against both the old and new implementations in sandboxes. When outputs diverged, the agents flagged the difference.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Engineers then reviewed those flagged cases before anything moved forward. After that human review stage, the validated version went into shadow-traffic testing against real production patterns.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Shadow traffic meaning real requests hitting both systems, but the new one is not actually serving the answers yet.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. The new version is listening and processing in parallel, but users are still getting responses from the original. It is a staged handoff. Sandbox comparison with agents, human review of the flags, shadow validation, then the switch.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the result?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Anthropic reports completing the migration without service downtime. Public traffic moved in September 2026. I want to be direct about the evidence here: this is Anthropic's own engineering documentation. Anthropic built both Claude and the system being migrated. Single attributed source, not independent measurement.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So we believe it happened. We are just being honest about who is doing the reporting.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That is the correct frame. Vendor engineering account of an internal production migration. The technical detail is specific and coherent. The source caveat stands.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I want to push on something, because if the agents compared all the outputs and found no meaningful differences, is that not simply sufficient? Why does the human review remain necessary?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Anthropic is quite direct about this in the write-up, and it is the part I find most worth dwelling on. Passing the local checker did not by itself establish that shipping was the right decision. The agents compared outputs systematically across the cases they covered. Human engineers applied judgment about whether the flagged differences mattered — whether the test cases were actually representative, and whether something significant might not have been tested at all.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The agents cannot know what they did not think to check.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly. The agent-driven comparison is thorough within its scope. Human review is what interrogates the scope itself. Those are different functions and both were structurally present in this workflow.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the agents close the volume gap and the engineers close the judgment gap.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That is the division. And neither is doing the other's job.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Can I try a hypothetical? Say someone listening is not running API migrations, but their team regularly updates internal data processing scripts. Does the same logic apply?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I want to be clear this is a proposed exercise, not a workflow with demonstrated results I can point to. But hypothetically, if you had an old and a new version of a script that handles, say, CSV formatting, you could construct something structurally similar. Build a set of synthetic edge cases covering the input conditions you care most about. Run both versions. Inspect the differences before accepting the new version. That is not the same scale as what Anthropic did — and you would need to define what behavioral equivalence actually means for your specific context before the comparison tells you anything useful.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Define the test before you run it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Define the test before you run it. That step comes before the tool. If you cannot say concretely what outputs matter and under which conditions, automated comparison returns noise, not confidence.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Jamie, I have to ask. Does it feel slightly strange to report on an AI company using their own AI to verify their own rewrite, and then publishing the account of it themselves?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It would feel stranger if the account were vague. The fact that Anthropic published specific technical details, including the explicit statement that passing the checker was not sufficient to make the shipping decision alone, is what makes this worth reporting rather than skipping. A press release saying we migrated successfully with AI is not interesting. An engineering write-up that volunteers its own limitation is a more honest document.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: They named what the agent could not do.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: They named it clearly. That is worth noting.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the technique is published even if the infrastructure is not.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That is the right distinction. The specific migration infrastructure Anthropic built for this is not a generally available product. The technique, using agents to systematically compare behavioral outputs between versions while keeping human review before anything ships, is a described approach that anyone working on a comparable verification problem can think about. The write-up is on Anthropic's research site.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I want to come back to what you said about the shadow-traffic stage, because that feels like the moment the whole thing becomes real. Up to that point, everything is a sandbox. The shadow test is the first time actual user requests are flowing through.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And it is the stage that could only happen after the sandbox comparison and human review were complete. The sequence is not arbitrary. Each stage is qualifying the next one. Sandbox comparison reduces the differences worth examining. Human review closes the judgment gaps the agents could not catch. Shadow traffic then tests behavioral equivalence against the actual distribution of real requests, which no synthetic test set fully replicates.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Three distinct checkpoints with different functions.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Three distinct checkpoints. The reason I think this changes how the work of building and maintaining software actually operates, not just one migration, is what it says about the verification bottleneck. The expensive part of a live behavioral rewrite has always been the gap between reading the code and knowing it behaves identically under conditions you did not fully model. Agent-driven comparison narrows that gap systematically in a way that manual spot-checking does not. It does not close the gap completely. Anthropic is explicit about that. But the shape of the remaining problem is different and more tractable.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the human is still on the other side of every flag that matters.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Still on the other side of every flag. The migration completed with public traffic in September 2026. The engineering write-up is Anthropic's own account, published November 25th, 2026. Single attributed source. Internal production context. Technique is published. Infrastructure is not generally available. The agents did the comparing, the engineers did the deciding —

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: and the API kept running throughout.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The API kept running throughout. That is quietly the whole story.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It is. That is the change.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's Jamie's AI transformation.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: We opened today asking why the president of the United States is flying to a construction site. Here's what we actually know.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Before we go — your question for today. We spent the whole week on agentic AI tools entering healthcare, finance, and retail. Yesterday we asked whether you'd trust an AI agent to manage your medical research or your shopping list. Today, given everything we talked about with chips, markets, and Washington scrutiny —

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: here's what we want to know:

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Thanks for spending the commute with us.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s question for you: If you had to choose, would you trust an AI agent to manage your home network security?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A quick final note: today’s episode was brought to you by The Ledger—decision-grade AI signal for people who cannot afford to be late.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What changed. Who wins. What you do next. That’s The AI Edge. Follow The AI Edge now. Join us next episode for what changes next.
